body.text: Global supply chains and geopolitical balances increasingly pivot around 2026, 2027 El Niño event. Tracking the primary facts helps separate durable structural shifts from daily noise.
The 2026, 2027 El Niño is the ongoing El Niño event, with its onset declared on 2 June 2026 by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

It is the strongest El Niño ever measured for its time of year, and the WMO has reported that it will likely be the strongest El Niño on record, with it already being classified as a "very strong El Niño", also known as a Super El Niño, and rarely called a "Behemoth" El Niño.
The 2026, 2027 El Niño is expected to peak in November or December and last through early 2027.
Background
A weak La Niña event evolved to ENSO-neutral in early 2026, but was rapidly transitioning to El Niño by May, according to Columbia University's Climate School.

Computer modeling in late May by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) suggested the development of an El Niño event was likely by the July through September peak of the Pacific hurricane season.

The Center for Climate Systems Research (CCSR) and the International Research Institute for Climate and Society (IRI) ENSO plume forecast gave a 98% probability of El Niño forming and a 97%-98% probability of continuing through the end of the year, a range Columbia called "remarkably high and narrow".

That month, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) confirmed the emergence of a strong El Niño, giving it a 63% chance of becoming intense enough by late fall and early winter to be one of the strongest on record.
On 8 October, NOAA stated that there was a greater than 83% chance that it would become the strongest El Niño on record by October-December.
Timeline
April
20 April, Columbia University's Climate School reports that the weak La Niña event had transitioned into an ENSO-neutral state.
May

21 May, Computer modeling by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) suggested the development of an El Niño event was likely by the July through September peak of the Pacific hurricane season.
June
The northern hemisphere summer temperatures in the east-central Pacific are among the highest on record, with NOAA predicting them to exceed those of past powerful El Niños.

2 June, The United Nations World Meteorological Organization (WMO) officially confirmed that El Niño conditions are actively developing in the tropical Pacific. This rapid transition follows a remarkably high 97, 98% probability forecast from Columbia University's Climate School.
11 June, A National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration notice stated that "El Niño conditions are present and expected to strengthen into the Northern Hemisphere winter 2026-27".
August

5 August, The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) issued a global seasonal update confirming that a developing El Niño event, combined with positive Indian Ocean Dipole conditions and record-warm global sea surface temperatures, is projected to drive above-normal temperatures globally throughout the August, October season.
98 °F) according to data from the Copernicus Climate Change Service, surpassing previous records driven by an intensifying El Niño and underlying global warming.
September

The WMO issued an unusually dire report that El Niño is "supersizing before our eyes" and forecast that it would likely be the strongest event since monitoring began. Records on El Niño magnitude date back to 1950.

September, which is considered to be the peak of the Atlantic hurricane season, has not seen a single Atlantic hurricane forming in the 2026 season, marking the latest season to feature no hurricanes since the first weather satellites were launched in the 1960s.

Typically, three hurricanes have already formed in the north Atlantic by late-September, but due to increased vertical wind shear, no hurricanes have formed in the Atlantic to date, the first season during the satellite era to do so, and breaking a more than a hundred-year-old record, the last season to feature no hurricanes during September was the 1914 season, which eventually did not record any hurricanes at all, although it is possible that some systems were undetected during that year.

In contrast, the Pacific season was hyperactive due to El Niño conditions, with the number of named storms in the northeastern by September Pacific being about 40% above average for this time of year.

Hawaii, an area that was previously hit by Hurricane Lala in August, was grazed by Hurricane Lowell and was also threatened by Hurricane Nolo. Elsewhere in the Eastern Pacific basin, Hurricane Polo hit western Mexico the same month, both Lowell and Polo peaked as Category 5 hurricanes, while Nolo peaked as a high-end Category 4.

4 Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI), which measures how far above the normal temperature a certain region of the Pacific surface has become, reached 2 °C, the NOAA's official criterion for a "very strong" El Niño event.

Monthly RONI values remain below 2 °C as of 15 September, a rolling average of three months of data is required to fully gauge the event. 4 SSTs of 3 °C since modern recording began in 1950, the other being the 2014-2016 El Nino.
October
4 region temperatures reach above 30°C for the first time in recorded history.
8 October, NOAA stated that there was a greater than 83% chance that the 2026-2027 El Niño would become the strongest El Niño on record by October-December.

9 October, Hurricane Isaias makes landfall near Destin, Florida with sustained winds of 105 miles per hour (169 km/h). It is the ninth named storm, first hurricane, and first major hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.

It ties the record for the latest date a first hurricane was recorded in the Atlantic basin since 1905. 37 m) above normal, with the approaching Tropical Storm Rachel adding to the flood risk. Several beachfront homes in the city of Redondo Beach are condemned.

21 October, UN Humanitarian Chief Tom Fletcher describes El Niño as a "Behemoth" during an appeal for aid for those affected by the ongoing El Nino, the first official to use the "Behemoth" adjective when addressing an El Nino event.
November

9 November, The WMO issued an updated assessment confirming that the strengthening El Niño was acting as a major risk multiplier alongside background global warming, pushing global climate indicators to near-record levels. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center maintained a high probability (>79%) of a strong-to-very strong event persisting through the early 2027 months.
Concurrently, humanitarian agencies highlighted mounting food security, drought, and flooding pressures linked to the developing event across East Africa and parts of Central America.
Preparations

The scale of this event notwithstanding, given that El Niño is a well-known phenomenon that has been studied for many decades, preparations can be made for specific geographic areas which have historically been impacted, particularly southern Africa.

On 4 June 2026, the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization and World Food Programme issued their first joint appeal for donations to avert a global humanitarian crisis. The World Meteorological Organization also urged preparation.
In mid-July, the NOAA gave 97% odds that a strong El Niño would persist through spring 2027.

The charity Americares, noting any strong El Niño's impact on the severity of heat, wildfires (and wildfire smoke), flooding, and hurricanes, termed the expected scenario as "a global shuffling of risk".

For example, Southern California anticipates severe rain and flooding, with the harbingers of unusually severe king tides already occurring in August whereas Australia anticipates drought and severe wildfires, and India expects an erratic, drier monsoon season.

Areas of Africa have barely recovered from the effects of the 2023, 2024 El Niño event, having experienced extreme floods and droughts. Oxfam is coordinating with other aid groups to shore up vital infrastructure such as electrical and water systems.
8 million people across 22 high-risk countries with anticipatory action funding for resilience projects to get ahead of the crisis.

China has launched a 100-day campaign to prepare for the effects of alternating severe rain, drought, and heat on agriculture and updating its early weather warning system, with cities being encouraged to draw up their own "climate risk" plans.

Policies are being changed from municipal down to the corporate level, with employers in the financial sector, for example, being mandated to provide public health measures, being at risk of prosecution if they fail to implement them.
